rows.text: For a set $A$ of positive integers and a real number $b>1$, write $$ X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{b^a-1}. $$ The series converges by comparison with a geometric series, since $(b^a-1)^{-1}\le b^{1-a}/(b-1)$. Erdős proved that the full series $X_{\mathbb{N}_{>0}}(b)$ is irrational at every integer base \[[5](#ref-erdos1948)\], and later obtained the same conclusion for pairwise coprime supports of finite reciprocal sum \[[7](#ref-erdos1968), p. 222\]. On that page he remarked that the coprimality assumption could be removed, and gave no details. For arbitrary infinite support in base two the question is Problem #257: **Problem 1.1 (Erdős \#257).** Is $X_A(2)$ irrational for every infinite $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{>0}$? We look for conditions on a support that every infinite subset inherits. The first replaces reciprocal summability by a weight that sees divisibility: for $a=2^km$ with $m$ odd, it charges $1/[m(b^{2^k}-1)]$ where reciprocal summability charges $1/(2^km)$, so that a large power of $2$ pays for many odd cofactors. More generally, we fix a finite set $P$ of primes and write $h(a)=\prod_{p\in P}p^{v_p(a)}$ for the *$P$-part* of $a$, where $v_p(a)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $a$. The prime powers may grow with $a$; the set of primes stays fixed. **Theorem 1.2 (a weighted condition on the support).** *Let $b\ge2$ be an integer, let $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ be infinite, and let $P$ be a finite nonempty set of primes. Set $h(a)=\prod_{p\in P}p^{v_p(a)}$. If* $$ W_{b,P}(A):=\sum_{a\in A} \frac{h(a)}{a(b^{h(a)}-1)}<\infty, \tag{1} $$ *then $X_A(b)$ is irrational. In particular, the base-two condition* $$ \sum_{a\in A}\frac{h(a)}{a(2^{h(a)}-1)}<\infty \tag{W} $$ *implies that $X_A(b)$ is irrational for every integer $b\ge2$. Both conclusions are hereditary under passage to infinite subsets.* For an example beyond reciprocal summability, consider the support $$ A_\star=\{2^km:k\ge1,\ m\text{ odd},\ m\le2^{2^k}\}. $$ For fixed $k$ the odd cofactors have reciprocal sum of order $2^k$, so the corresponding terms contribute at least $1/4$ to $\sum_{a\in A_\star}1/a$ and at most $2^{1-k}$ to [(W)](#eq:weighted-return); Section [2](#sec:eight-return-extensions) proves both bounds. Hence every infinite subset of $A_\star$ has an irrational value at every integer base, although $A_\star$ has divergent reciprocal sum. Since $h/(2^h-1)\le1$, the theorem also contains the reciprocal-summable case, and Section [A](#sec:reciprocal-support) gives a direct proof of the extension Erdős stated. The second condition uses the joint divisibility of the exponents: it bounds fractional powers of divisor counts by positive divisor sums (Theorem [3.1](#thm:variable-fractional-cover)). The two conditions are incomparable, and they combine. If $E$ satisfies the base-two weighted condition and $V$ has a summable divisor cover, then every infinite subset of $E\cup V$ has an irrational sum (Theorem [4.1](#res:mixed-supports)). Since two irrational subseries may add up to a rational number, the proof has to control both errors at the same index. The separating constructions of Proposition [5.1](#res:weighted-cover-incomparability) produce such a union that lies outside both individual classes (Corollary [5.2](#res:strict-mixed-supports)). All three criteria are sufficient conditions; none of them characterises the supports in Problem [1.1](#res:problem). Every proof compares a multiple of $X_A(b)$ with an integer. For a positive integer $N$ we put $$ \Delta_{b,A}(N)=\sum_{a\in A}\frac{b^{N\bmod a}-1}{b^a-1} =(b^N-1)X_A(b)-J_{b,A}(N),\qquad J_{b,A}(N)=\sum_{\substack{a\in A\\a\le N}} \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor N/a\rfloor}b^{N-ja}. \tag{D} $$ The identity follows on dividing $N$ by each $a$. At an integer base $J_{b,A}(N)$ is an integer, and for infinite $A$ the displacement $\Delta_{b,A}(N)$ is positive, because some $a\in A$ exceeds $N$. Hence, if $X_A(b)=p/q$ with $p\in\mathbb Z$ and $q\ge1$ an integer, then $q\Delta_{b,A}(N)$ is a positive integer and $\Delta_{b,A}(N)\ge1/q$. It therefore suffices to find displacements tending to zero. The displacement is a positive real number and may exceed $1$, so it should be distinguished from a fractional part; Erdős also proposed working with fractional parts of powers times the value of the series \[[7](#ref-erdos1968), p. 226\]. To make the displacement small we take $N$ to be a multiple of a modulus. Divisibility then cancels the finitely many exponents that divide the modulus, and the remaining terms have small means over a complete period when their gcd with the modulus is large. The bound for an incomplete period lacks the factor $1/a$, and averaging over dyadic lengths restores it: an exponent enters the truncated error only once the sampled range reaches it, and the reciprocals of the later lengths form a geometric tail bounded by a multiple of $1/a$. Exponents beyond the sampled range are estimated separately. Because every bound depends explicitly on the modulus, both criteria can share one average. Sections [2](#sec:eight-return-extensions)–[4](#sec:mixed) prove the three criteria, and Sections [5](#sec:comparison)–[6](#sec:map) separate their support classes and describe the limits of the method. The appendices give the direct proof for reciprocal-summable supports, the exact denominators of finite subseries, and tests for whether a prescribed rational number is a subseries sum; these tests decide neither $1/2$ nor $1/21$.

rows.label: sec-rational-membership
rows.text: The preceding results start from a support and prove irrationality. We now fix a target value and ask whether some support represents it. The first recurrence below is a necessary condition for a rational value, and the greedy recurrence then gives an exact criterion for membership; neither supplies the arithmetic information still missing for $1/2$ and $1/21$. ### C.1 Rational values and scaled tails Suppose $X_A(2)=p/v$, where $p\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $v\ge1$ is an integer. Multiplying the coefficient-series identity by $v2^N$ gives $$ z_N:=v\sum_{r\ge1}c_A(N+r)2^{-r} =2^Np-v\sum_{n=1}^{N}c_A(n)2^{N-n}\in\mathbb{Z}. $$ Separating the first term of the tail then gives $z_{N+1}=2z_N-vc_A(N+1)$, in which every coefficient $c_A(n)$ is a divisor count of the same set $A$. For nonempty $A$, any $a_0=\min A$ consecutive integers contain a multiple of $a_0$, so the runs of zeros in $c_A$ have length at most $a_0-1$. For infinite $A$ we choose $k$ exponents and a common multiple $L$; then $c_A(L)\ge k$, and the scaled tail satisfies $\sum_{r\ge1}c_A(L-1+r)2^{-r}\ge k/2$. Thus the scaled tails are unbounded. The compatibility condition on the coefficients is the Dirichlet convolution identity $\mu*c_A=\mathbf1_A$, where $\mu$ is the Möbius function, so a putative recurrence with integral forcing must satisfy $(\mu*c_A)(n)\in\{0,1\}$ for all $n$. The telescoping proof of the integer-recurrence criterion and the Möbius inversion argument are given under [Bounds for a general coefficient sequence](../long/reasoning-record.md#record257:coefficient-recurrence) in the companion paper, whose example $A=\{2\}$ has value $1/3$. The correspondence admits finite supports, so a counterexample to Problem [1.1](#res:problem) must in addition be infinite. ### C.2 The achievement set Let $w_n=(2^n-1)^{-1}$ and $$ \mathcal A=\left\{\sum_{n\ge1}\varepsilon_nw_n: \varepsilon_n\in\{0,1\}\right\},\qquad R_N=\sum_{n>N}w_n. $$ The estimate $$ 2^{-N}0$, which proves uniqueness. Since every weight exceeds its tail, Hornich’s theorem \[[15](#ref-hornich1941)\], as proved by Nitecki \[[10](#ref-nitecki2013), Theorem 4(1), p. 9\], shows that $\mathcal A$ is a Cantor set of measure $\lim_N2^NR_N$, and the estimate above gives $2^NR_N\to1$, so $\lambda(\mathcal A)=1$. Concretely, fixing the first $N$ digits gives $2^N$ disjoint closed intervals of length $R_N$; these unions decrease to $\mathcal A$, and continuity of Lebesgue measure from above gives the same limit. Kovač and Tao record this strict-tail inequality and the Cantor conclusion in the fixed-base setting \[[4](#ref-kovactao), Remark 4.1\]. The [geometry section of the companion paper](../long/reasoning-record.md#record257:geometry) also treats restricted supports. For any allowed set $J$ of exponents, removing exponents can only decrease the tail of each retained weight, so the same inequality gives injectivity. If $J$ omits exactly the finite set $F$, its achievement set has measure $2^{-|F|}$, and if $J$ omits infinitely many exponents, the measure is zero. ### C.3 The greedy recurrence For $x\ge0$ the greedy rule starts with $r_0=x$ and, at each rank $n\ge1$, selects $n$ when $r_{n-1}\ge(2^n-1)^{-1}$, in which case it subtracts that weight. Let $A_x$ be the resulting support and $c_x(n)=\#\{a\in A_x:a\mid n\}$, and set $$ P_0=0,\qquad P_{N+1}=2P_N+c_x(N+1),\qquad Q_N=\lfloor2^Nx\rfloor-P_N. $$ Here $P_N=\sum_{j=1}^N2^{N-j}c_x(j)$ truncates the coefficient series [(6)](#eq:incidence), whereas $r_N$ truncates the selected Lambert weights: $Q_N$ measures the error of coefficient truncation, and $r_N$ is the real remainder after $N$ greedy decisions. The bound $P_N\le2^NX_{A_x}(2)\le2^Nx$ gives $Q_N\ge0$, and $$ Q_{N+1}=2Q_N+\beta_N-c_x(N+1),\qquad \beta_N=\lfloor2^{N+1}x\rfloor-2\lfloor2^Nx\rfloor\in\{0,1\}. \tag{10} $$ The recurrence is integral for every real target. Writing $\delta=x-X_{A_x}(2)\ge0$, we obtain from the coefficient expansion $$ Q_N=\left\lfloor 2^N\delta+ \sum_{r\ge1}c_x(N+r)2^{-r}\right\rfloor. $$ For a represented target $\delta=0$ and $Q_N=O(\sqrt N)$, which leaves too little room for unit increases throughout a long window. For an unrepresented target, $2^N\delta$ eventually dominates the divisor count in the recurrence and forces strict increase. The theorem below makes both halves precise. **Theorem C.1 (membership and nonincreasing integer remainders).** *For every real $x\ge0$, the following are equivalent:* $$ \begin{gathered} x\in\mathcal A;\\ \forall K\ge0\ \exists N\ge K:\quad Q_{N+1}\le Q_N;\\ \forall K\ge0\ \exists N\in[K,K+2\lfloor\sqrt K\rfloor+12): \quad Q_{N+1}\le Q_N. \end{gathered} $$ *Proof.* For a represented target the remaining sum is at least $w_n$ exactly when $n$ belongs to the representing support, since $R_n0$ and $Q_N\ge2^N\delta-1$, which eventually exceeds $c_x(N+1)\le N+1$. Equation [(10)](#eq:actual-repair-recurrence) then makes $Q_N$ strictly increasing, contradicting the cofinal nonincreases. ◻ The nonincreases must occur along the target’s own greedy sequence. For $x=0$ no exponent is selected and $Q_N=0$ at every rank, and every finite subseries sum is likewise represented and satisfies the criterion. The target $x=3/4$ lies strictly between $R_1<2/3$ and $w_1=1$, so it is unrepresented and its integer remainders eventually increase strictly. For $1/2$ and $1/21$ the theorem leaves open which alternative occurs. An ordinary extension of the argument, beyond the square-root window proved in Lean, gives a uniform subpower window: for each $0<\varepsilon<1$, a window of length $\lceil C_\varepsilon(K+1)^\varepsilon\rceil$ suffices for a suitable constant $C_\varepsilon$. Indeed, $\tau(n)\le A_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon$ gives $Q_N\le D_\varepsilon(N+1)^\varepsilon$ for represented targets, where $D_\varepsilon=A_\varepsilon\sum_{r\ge1}r^\varepsilon2^{-r}$. Choose $C_\varepsilon>D_\varepsilon(C_\varepsilon+3)^\varepsilon$, which is possible because $\varepsilon<1$. For $T=\lceil C_\varepsilon(K+1)^\varepsilon\rceil$, strict increase at all $T$ steps would give $$ T\le Q_{K+T}\le D_\varepsilon(K+T+1)^\varepsilon \le D_\varepsilon(C_\varepsilon+3)^\varepsilon(K+1)^\varepsilon $$ \forall K\ \exists N\ge K:\qquad c_x(N+1)\ge Q_N+\beta_N, \qquad x\in\{1/2,1/21\}. \tag{11} $$ Here $Q_N$ and $c_x$ must arise from the same greedy support $A_x$. The companion paper keeps counterexamples to fixed-multiplier schedules, with their finite phase masks; they concern those schedules only and decide neither target.

rows.label: sec-reciprocal-support
rows.text: Erdős stated the following extension of his pairwise-coprime theorem \[[7](#ref-erdos1968), p. 222\]. It follows from Theorem [1.2](#res:weighted-support), since $h/(2^h-1)\le1$, but a direct argument shows why reciprocal summability makes the averaging simpler. **Theorem A.1 (reciprocal-summable supports).** *Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ be infinite. If* $$ \sum_{a\in A}\frac1a<\infty, $$ *then $X_A(b)$ is irrational for every integer $b\ge2$.* Erdős also discussed weaker conditions \[[7](#ref-erdos1968), pp. 222, 226\]; we make no identification of our weighted hypothesis with the conditions he suggested. Reciprocal summability permits two successive limits. First the observation length grows while the modulus stays fixed, and then the modulus grows until each fixed exponent divides it. The two interchanges of limit and sum use different summable bounds, and neither requires the infinite support to have a period. Fix the integer base $b\ge2$ and put $$ w_{b,d}(N)=\frac{b^{N\bmod d}}{b^d-1},\qquad T_N^{(b)}=\sum_{d\in A}w_{b,d}(N). $$ Then $T_N^{(b)}-T_0^{(b)}=\Delta_{b,A}(N)$. For a fixed positive integer $Q$, the orbit of $Q$ modulo $d$ consists of $d/g$ residues, where $g=(Q,d)$, and summing the geometric progression gives $$ M_{Q,b}(d):=\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1X\sum_{m=1}^Xw_{b,d}(Qm) =\frac{g}{d(b^g-1)}\le\frac1d. \tag{8} $$ In the example $b=2$, $Q=4$, $d=6$ of Section [2](#sec:eight-return-extensions), the mean is $1/9$ for $w_{2,6}$ and $2/21$ for its displacement. When $d\mid Q$ we have $w_{b,d}(Qm)=w_{b,d}(0)$, and the displacement vanishes. To interchange the sum over exponents with this limit, we need a bound that is summable in $d$ for the fixed modulus $Q$. Counting positive multiples of $d$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} \frac1X\sum_{m=1}^Xw_{b,d}(Qm) &=\sum_{r\ge1}b^{-r} \frac{\#\{1\le m\le X:d\mid Qm+r\}}X\\ &\le\sum_{r\ge1}b^{-r}\frac{Q+r}{d} =\frac{Q/(b-1)+b/(b-1)^2}{d}\le\frac{Q+2}{d}. \end{aligned} $$ Indeed, the counted multiples are distinct and at most $QX+r$. For this fixed $Q$ the majorant $(Q+2)/d$ is summable over $A$, so dominated convergence takes the limit in the observation length inside the sum over $d$ and gives the Cesàro mean $\sum_{d\in A}M_{Q,b}(d)$. The majorant deteriorates as $Q$ grows, which is why a second limit is needed. Next let $Q_t=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,t)$. For each fixed $d$ we eventually have $d\mid Q_t$ and $M_{Q_t,b}(d)=(b^d-1)^{-1}$, and a second dominated-convergence argument, now with the bound $M_{Q_t,b}(d)\le1/d$, yields $$ \sum_{d\in A}M_{Q_t,b}(d)\longrightarrow X_A(b). \tag{9} $$ Hence the limiting displacement means tend to zero. We choose $t$, then a sufficiently long finite average, and then a term no larger than that average. The resulting arbitrarily small positive displacements contradict the bound $1/q$ that [(D)](#eq:intro-displacement) gives under rationality, and this proves Theorem [A.1](#res:reciprocal-support) at every integer base. For example, the powerful integers (those whose prime exponents are all at least two) have the form $u^2v^3$, so their reciprocal sum is at most $\zeta(2)\zeta(3)$, and the theorem applies to every infinite set of powerful integers. For the full set of perfect powers, compare Duverney and Tachiya \[[1](#ref-duverneytachiya), Corollary 1.2, p. 4\] and the earlier linear-independence results of Luca and Tachiya \[[13](#ref-lucatachiya2014independence)\].

rows.label: app-answers
rows.text:
*Question [1](#chk:hypotheses).* Only $\{2,4,8,16,\dots\}$: $\{2,4\}$ is finite (its sum $\tfrac25$ is rational), and for $\{2,4,6,\dots\}$ the sum $\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac16+\dots$ is half of $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\dots$, which diverges.

*Question [2](#chk:positive).* In the identity $R(k)=((2^k-1)p-qJ(k))/q$ the numerator is an integer, so if it is positive it is at least $1$, and $R(k)\ge1/q$. Choosing $k$ using $q$ leaves this argument intact, because $2^k-1$ and $J(k)$ are still integers. The value zero would give no contradiction. Infinitude supplies a selected $n>k$, whose multiplied term is positive and less than $1$ and so contributes all of itself to $R(k)$, while the other contributions are nonnegative.

*Question [3](#chk:columns).* The exponents $A$ and the original sum $S$ stay fixed, while the multiplier changes from $15$ to $255$, and within a column every selected term is transformed by the same multiplier. The row minima may come from different columns, and then no single multiplier applied to $S$ produces them.

*Question [4](#chk:partial).* A consecutive cycle has total below $1$ and $n$ entries, hence mean below $1/n$. A sampled cycle selects the smallest remainder from each group of equal size, and since the fractional parts increase with the remainder, its mean is no larger, even when it has fewer entries. The first value alone, however, is $\tfrac{15}{63}=\tfrac5{21}=\tfrac{10}{42}$, which exceeds $\tfrac16=\tfrac7{42}$. The bound for complete cycles may fail for a beginning portion, and the separate bound [(6)](#eq:uniform-main) is there to cover such portions.

*Question [5](#chk:order).* No, since $2Q'/T=128/512=1/4>1/10$. We must choose $T$ again: $T'=1024$ still fails, but $T'=2048$ works, since $128/2048=1/16<1/10$. The middle exponents $32,64,\dots,2048$ now have cycle lengths $1,1,2,4,8,16,32$, so $M=64$ still works, although its validity had to be rechecked even though its value did not change. This is why $Q$ is fixed before $T$.

*Exercise [1](#ex:2).* The first five entries sum to $26/31$ and the next two to $4/31$, so all seven average $30/217$. The two piece-means, $26/155$ and $2/31$, must be weighted by their lengths, $\bigl(5\cdot\tfrac{26}{155}+2\cdot\tfrac2{31}\bigr)/7=30/217$, since equal weights for the two pieces would give each entry of the shorter piece more weight than each entry of the longer one.

*Exercise [2](#ex:3).* Both $3$ and $6$ divide $12$, so $7$ and $63$ divide $2^{12}-1=4095$. The remainder of $12$ on division by $5$ is $2$, so the remainder on division by $31$ is $2^2-1=3$; indeed $4095=31\times132+3$.

*Exercise [3](#ex:4).* For $k=3^j$, the exponents $3^i$ with $i\le j$ divide $k$ and leave nothing. Each later exponent $n=3^i$ leaves less than $\tfrac2{2^{n-k}}$, and the gaps $3^i-3^j$ are distinct and at least $2\times3^j$, so $R(3^j)<\sum_{e\ge2\times3^j}\tfrac2{2^e}=\tfrac4{2^{2\times3^j}}$, which is below $\tfrac1q$ for large $j$.

*Exercise [4](#ex:5).* We have $(\sqrt2-1)^2=3-2\sqrt2$, $(\sqrt2-1)(3-2\sqrt2)=5\sqrt2-7$ and $(a\sqrt2-c)(3-2\sqrt2)=(3a+2c)\sqrt2-(4a+3c)$. Starting from $\sqrt2-1=1\sqrt2-1$, the last recurrence preserves nonnegative integer values of $a$ and $c$, so every odd power $(\sqrt2-1)^{2i+1}$ is $m\sqrt2-j$ for nonnegative integers $m$ and $j$, and it is positive. Since $1^2<2<(3/2)^2$, we have $0<\sqrt2-1<\tfrac12$, and hence $0<(\sqrt2-1)^{2i+1}<\tfrac1{2\cdot4^i}$, which is below $\tfrac1q$ once $2\cdot4^i>q$. By the test, $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

*Exercise [5](#ex:6).* (a) With $P_0=1$, $a_j=P_{j-1}+1$ and $P_j=P_{j-1}a_j$, so $\tfrac1{P_{j-1}}-\tfrac1{P_j}=\tfrac{a_j-1}{P_j}=\tfrac1{a_j}$, and adding these for $1,\dots,j$ leaves $1-\tfrac1{P_j}$. Since $P_j\ge2^j$, these partial sums tend to $1$, so the infinite set $A$ satisfies the reciprocal-sum hypothesis of the theorem. (b) The first $j$ exponents divide $P_j$, and the exponent $P_j+1$ exceeds $k=P_j$, so it leaves $\tfrac{2^{P_j}-1}{2^{P_j+1}-1}$, which is at least $\tfrac37$ because $7(2^{P_j}-1)-3(2^{P_j+1}-1)=2^{P_j}-4\ge0$. Thus the particular choices $k=P_j$ fail to make the remainders small. Other multiples of $P_j$ preserve the same initial zeros, and averaging lets us search among them.

rows.label: app-full
rows.text: This appendix supplies the details on convergence and limits, the divisibility argument for sampled cycles, the estimates at other bases, and an optional comparison with the formal proof. ### A.1 Convergence and tails For nonnegative terms $a_n$, the partial sums $\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n$ increase. If they are bounded above, let $L$ be their least upper bound, the smallest real number that is at least every partial sum. For every $\varepsilon>0$ some partial sum exceeds $L-\varepsilon$, for otherwise $L-\varepsilon$ would be a smaller upper bound, and every later partial sum then lies in $(L-\varepsilon,L]$, so the series converges to $L$. Its tail after $N$ equals $L-\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n$ and tends to zero, which is the property used twice when choosing the cutoffs in Section [7](#sec:proof). Comparison of series follows by comparing partial sums: if $0\le a_n\le b_n$ and $\sum b_n<\infty$, then $\sum a_n\le\sum b_n<\infty$, and if one term is strictly smaller, the sums differ by at least that positive difference. In particular, restricting a nonnegative series to a subset of its indices can only decrease its sum. For $0 ### A.2 Passing to the full transformed sum Fix $k$. Each $\ell_n(k)$ is nonnegative and at most $(2^k-1)/(2^n-1)$, so $R(k)$ converges by comparison with $(2^k-1)S$, and only selected exponents $n\le k$ have nonzero integer parts. For any integer $L\ge k$, splitting the finitely many terms up to $L$ gives $$ (2^k-1)\sum_{\substack{n\in A\\n\le L}}\frac1{2^n-1} =J(k)+\sum_{\substack{n\in A\\n\le L}}\ell_n(k). $$ As $L$ grows, $J(k)$ stays fixed and the two partial sums tend to $S$ and $R(k)$, which proves [(3)](#eq:split-main). ### A.3 Why the sampled remainders form a cycle The elementary cancellation fact states that if positive integers $c,u$ are coprime and $c$ divides $du$, then $c$ divides $d$. The example in Section [6.2](#sec:cycles) used $c=3$ and $u=2$, and for general coprime $c,u$ the same argument uses integers $a,b$ with $au+bc=1$. To see that they exist, let $v$ be the smallest positive value of $au+bc$ as $a,b$ range over the integers; there is at least one positive value, since $u=1\cdot u+0\cdot c$. Write $v=au+bc$ with coefficients attaining this minimum. Division gives $u=sv+r$ with $0\le r ### A.4 Adding the row averages For finitely many rows $n\le H$, adding the row averages is the same as averaging the column totals, since both operations add the same entries and divide by $M$. Keep $Q$ and $M$ fixed. Given any positive target $\varepsilon$, each of the $M$ convergent column sums $R(mQ)$ has tail less than $\varepsilon$ beyond some row cutoff, and beyond the largest of these finitely many cutoffs all column tails, and therefore their average, are less than $\varepsilon$. Consequently the finite sums of row averages tend to the average of the full column totals. This proves [(4)](#eq:average-main) with only finite rearrangements. ### A.5 Other bases Let $b\ge2$ be an integer; for $b=3$, the exponents $2,4,8,\dots$ give $1/8+1/80+1/6560+\dots$. Convergence and the fractional-part formula carry over, because $b^n-1\ge2^{n-1}$ and $b^{k+n}-1=b^k(b^n-1)+(b^k-1)$. For a consecutive cycle, the sum of the fractional parts is $$ \frac{(b^0-1)+\dots+(b^{n-1}-1)}{b^n-1} <\frac{b^0+b^1+\dots+b^{n-1}}{b^n-1} =\frac1{b-1}\le1. $$ Here we used $1+b+\dots+b^{n-1}=(b^n-1)/(b-1)$ and $b\ge2$. The fractional parts still increase with the remainder, so the comparison by equal groups bounds the average over a complete sampled cycle by the average over a consecutive cycle, which is below $1/n$. For $n\ge2$ the $n-1$ positive entries still increase and have total less than $1$, so the argument for beginning portions in Section [6.3](#sec:unfinished) gives the same bound $2/n$ for consecutive entries starting at $k=1$, and keeping only the sampled entries gives the bound $2Q/n$ for every sampled length $M$. For $n=1$ the fractional parts are all zero, because $(b^k-1)/(b-1)$ is an integer. Both estimates needed for the three groups therefore remain valid, and with the same choices of $t,Q,T,M$ the proof shows that $\sum_{n\in A}1/(b^n-1)$ is irrational whenever $A$ is infinite and $\sum_{n\in A}1/n<\infty$ \[[6](#ref-shortpaper), Theorem A.1\]. ### A.6 The formal proof and how it differs The theorem is proved in Lean as [`irrational_erdosSupportSeries_of_summable_reciprocal`](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/436f55ebdafa67e4af0fff79f621c13f2ded12bf/lean/Erdos249257/AllBaseReciprocalSupportIrrationality.lean#L395). For every natural number $b\ge2$ and every infinite set $A$ of natural numbers whose sequence of terms $1/n$ for $n\in A$ (and $0$ otherwise) is summable, it states that the sum of $1/(b^n-1)$ over $A$ is irrational. Lean’s natural numbers start at $0$, and in Lean division by $0$ gives $0$, so the exponent $0$ contributes $0$ to both sums; removing it changes neither sum and leaves an infinite set infinite. At $b=2$ the statement is therefore Theorem [1](#thm:main), and in general it is the formal version of \[[6](#ref-shortpaper), Theorem A.1\]. The Lean kernel accepts the proof, and a [Comparator check](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/846d57d3f9926696332d782eb232aaf3cf803a99/evidence/erdos-257-mersenne-support-subseries.md#res-reciprocal-support-comparator) confirms, with a second independent kernel checker, that the proof establishes a separately written formal statement. The finite reconstruction in Sections [3](#sec:test)–[7](#sec:proof) and its estimates are ordinary proofs written for this exposition; the formal proof follows its own route and does not check them line by line. At base $2$ the Lean proof follows \[[6](#ref-shortpaper), Appendix A\] and takes limits of averages; it reaches the other bases by comparing each base-$b$ fractional part with twice the base-$2$ one, a different route from Appendix [A.5](#app:bases). With the exponent $0$ omitted, the shifted quantity used in Lean is $$ \sum_{n\in A}\frac{2^{k\bmod n}}{2^n-1}=S_A+R(k), $$ whose value at $k=0$ is $S_A$, so a value strictly between $S_A$ and $S_A+\varepsilon$ means $0t}1/n$, which tends to zero. To obtain one witness it chooses a suitable $Q$ first and a sufficiently long average second. Our cutoffs $t,T$ and number $M$ of columns make those choices explicit, using the separately proved estimate $2Q/n$, and under the rationality assumption both arguments make the integer $qR(k)$ lie strictly between $0$ and $1$.

rows.label: sec-doubling
rows.text:
We return to the opening example, $A=\{2,4,8,16,\dots\}$, and can now see why $255$ cleared the first three terms: it is $2^8-1$, and the exponents $2,4,8$ all divide $8$. In the new notation the calculation reads
$$
255S=103+R(8),\qquad R(8)=\frac1{257}+\frac1{16843009}+\dots>0.
$$
One small remainder rules out only some denominators, and to rule out every $q$ we need remainders as small as we please. For any doubling exponent $k$, all selected $n\le k$ divide $k$ and contribute zero, while every later selected exponent $n$ is at least $2k$ and gives
$$
0<\ell_n(k)=\frac{2^k-1}{2^n-1}
 <\frac{2^k}{2^{n-1}}=\frac2{2^{n-k}}.
$$
For $k=8$ the gaps $n-k$ are $8,24,56,\dots$, and in general they are distinct integers at least $k$. Inserting the missing positive terms, so that the gaps run through *all* integers $k,k+1,k+2,\dots$, can only increase the upper bound, and so
$$
0<R(k)<\sum_{e=k}^{\infty}\frac2{2^e}=\frac4{2^k}.
$$
The last equality is the formula for a geometric series whose first term is $2/2^k$ and whose ratio is $1/2$.

For $k=8$ this gives $R(8)<1/64$, which rules out every denominator $q\le64$, since such a denominator would force $R(8)\ge1/q\ge1/64$; for $k=16$ the bound is $R(16)<1/16384$. Given any proposed denominator $q$, we choose a doubling exponent $k$ with $2^k>4q$, and then $0<R(k)<1/q$ contradicts rationality. This completes the proof for the doubling exponents.

What made this work is that each $k$ both eliminated all earlier terms and left the next exponent at least $2k$. A general set $A$ need not have that spacing, and the next section explains how averaging takes its place.

rows.label: sec-exercises
rows.text: **Question 1.** Which of $\{2,4\}$, $\{2,4,8,16,\dots\}$ and $\{2,4,6,8,\dots\}$ does Theorem [1](#thm:main) apply to? **Question 2.** Suppose that $S=p/q$. Why is $00$, and where does the infinitude of $A$ supply it? **Question 3.** In the square-exponent table, what stays fixed and what changes when we move from $k=4$ to $k=8$? Why may we not choose the smallest entry in each row and treat their sum as one successful attempt? **Question 4.** Why is the mean over a complete consecutive cycle below $1/n$? Why does the same bound hold for a complete sampled cycle, which may have fewer than $n$ entries? For $n=6$ and $Q=4$, the full cycle averages $\tfrac2{21}<\tfrac16$. Is the first value alone also below $\tfrac16$? **Question 5.** In Section [7.1](#app:numbers), replace $Q=16$ by $Q'=64$ and keep $T=512$. Does the far bound still give less than $\tfrac1{10}$? What must be chosen again? **Exercise 1.** For $n=5$ and $Q=1$, calculate the mean of the first seven entries by separating them into a complete cycle and a beginning portion of the next. Why is the mean of all seven different from half the sum of the two piece-means? **Exercise 2.** Use the fractional-part formula [(2)](#eq:fracpart-main) to show that $2^{12}-1$ is divisible by $7$ and by $63$, and find its remainder on division by $2^5-1=31$. **Exercise 3.** Adapt the proof in Section [5](#sec:doubling) to the exponents $3,9,27,81,\dots$, using $k=3^j$. **Exercise 4.** Show that $5\sqrt2-7=(\sqrt2-1)^3$, and that multiplying a number $a\sqrt2-c$, where $a,c$ are nonnegative integers, by $3-2\sqrt2$ gives another number $a'\sqrt2-c'$, where $a',c'$ are nonnegative integers. Use the test of Section [3](#sec:test) to show that $\sqrt2$ is irrational. **Exercise 5.** Let $a_1=2$ and let each later exponent be one more than the product of the earlier ones, giving $2,3,7,43,1807,\dots$. Set $A=\{a_1,a_2,\dots\}$ and write $P_j=a_1a_2\cdots a_j$. (a) Show that $\tfrac1{a_1}+\dots+\tfrac1{a_j}=1-\tfrac1{P_j}$. (b) Show that with $k=P_j$ the first $j$ exponents leave $0$ but the exponent $P_j+1$ leaves at least $\tfrac37$, so $R(P_j)\ge\tfrac37$ for every $j$.

rows.label: sec-general
rows.text: ##### Larger multipliers need not help. For the square exponents $A=\{1,4,9,16,\dots\}$, both $k=4$ and $k=8$ are divisible by the first two selected exponents $1$ and $4$, and all later selected exponents exceed $8$, so their integer parts vanish for both multipliers. Consequently $$ R(4)=15\left(\frac1{511}+\frac1{65535}+\dots\right),\qquad R(8)=255\left(\frac1{511}+\frac1{65535}+\dots\right)=17R(4). $$ In fact $R(4)\approx0.0296$ and $R(8)\approx0.503$: increasing $k$ while keeping the same zero contributions has enlarged the remaining terms. Eliminating longer initial groups need not help either. In Exercise [5](#ex:6) the next selected exponent is $k+1$, which leaves $(2^k-1)/(2^{k+1}-1)$, close to $1/2$. What matters is which values of $k$ we use, and the number of initial rows they make zero is only part of the story. ### 6.1 One table, many attempts Keep $A$, and hence the original number $S$, fixed. For each new choice of $k$ we repeat the whole calculation: multiply every selected term by $2^k-1$, subtract its integer part, and add what remains to obtain $R(k)$. *Each column below is one complete attempt at the contradiction*, and each row follows the contribution of one original term across the attempts. We need one column whose total is less than $1/q$. We choose candidate exponents spaced $Q$ apart, $k=Q,2Q,\dots,MQ$, so that $Q$ is the spacing, $M$ is the number of attempts, $m$ labels the attempt $k=mQ$, and the multiplier itself is $2^{mQ}-1$. Neither $Q$ nor $k$ has to belong to $A$. We take $Q$ divisible by an initial group of selected exponents, so that those rows stay zero in every column. For the square exponents, $Q=4$ gives the following table. | | | | | | |:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:| | selected exponent $n$ | $k=4$ | $k=8$ | $k=12$ | $k=16$ | | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | | $4$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | | $9$ | $15/511$ | $255/511$ | $7/511$ | $127/511$ | | $16$ | $15/65535$ | $255/65535$ | $4095/65535$ | $0$ | | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | | column total | $R(4)$ | $R(8)$ | $R(12)$ | $R(16)$ | Every entry is a fractional part $\ell_n(k)$; for example, the cell $n=9,k=12$ uses $12=1\cdot9+3$, so $\ell_9(12)=(2^3-1)/(2^9-1)=7/511$. Each column uses the same multiplier throughout, including in the rows not displayed (Question [3](#chk:columns)). ##### Average complete attempts. Different rows may be small in different columns, and choosing a separate column for each row would give no single multiplier for the original series. Instead we average *every row across the same columns* and then add the row averages. The result is the average of the complete column totals, since both calculations add the same entries and divide by the same number $M$. In symbols, $$ \frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}R(mQ) =\sum_{n\in A}\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}\ell_n(mQ). \tag{4} $$ With infinitely many rows we first use finite portions and then let them grow, and convergence preserves the equality (Appendix [A.4](#app:proof)). If this average is below $1/q$, then at least one whole column has total below $1/q$, for otherwise every column total would be at least $1/q$ and so would their average. ##### What the two estimates will do. We shall divide the rows into three groups. An initial finite group stays zero. A further finite group can complete its cycles if $M$ is chosen suitably, and we shall bound the average of each such row by $1/n$. For the infinitely many remaining rows we need a bound valid for every $M$, and we shall prove the bound $2Q/n$. Once $Q$ is fixed, the sum of these bounds becomes as small as we like if we move far enough down the rows, because the remaining reciprocals $1/n$ have arbitrarily small total. Section [7](#sec:proof) chooses the two row cutoffs, and then $M$, so that both nonzero groups have small total averages. ### 6.2 Complete cycles give small averages To find a rule for every row we look at $n=3$ and $n=6$, even though they are not exponents of the square series. Start with $n=3$ and consecutive $k$: | | | | | | | | |:--------------|:-------:|:-------:|:-----:|:-------:|:-------:|:-----:| | $k$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | | $k\bmod3$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | | $\ell_3(k)$ | $1/7$ | $3/7$ | $0$ | $1/7$ | $3/7$ | $0$ | One repeating block, or *cycle*, has sum $4/7<1$ and average $4/21<1/3$. The bound concerns the average only, since one entry, $3/7$, exceeds $1/3$. For general $n$, a consecutive cycle has the remainders $0,1,\dots,n-1$. The powers $2^0,2^1,\dots,2^{n-1}$ add up to $2^n-1$, which is the denominator, and each numerator is one less than the corresponding power, so the total over the cycle is $$ \frac{(2^0-1)+(2^1-1)+\dots+(2^{n-1}-1)}{2^n-1} <\frac{2^0+2^1+\dots+2^{n-1}}{2^n-1}=1. $$ Dividing by its $n$ entries gives a cycle average below $1/n$. These reciprocals bound the row averages, and that is why the hypothesis $\sum_{n\in A}1/n<\infty$ controls their sum. ##### Keep the required spacing. Our candidates move in steps of $Q$, because the spacing $Q$ is what preserves the initial zero rows. With $n=6$ and $Q=4$ we find | | | | | |:--------------------|:---------:|:--------:|:------:| | sample number $m$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | | $k=4m$ | $4$ | $8$ | $12$ | | $k\bmod6$ | $4$ | $2$ | $0$ | | $\ell_6(k)$ | $15/63$ | $3/63$ | $0$ | The last two rows repeat every three samples, only the even remainders occur, and the average is $(15+3+0)/(3\cdot63)=2/21<1/6$. Let $g=\gcd(n,Q)$ be the *greatest common divisor*, the largest positive integer dividing both $n$ and $Q$, and put $c=n/g$. In the example $n=6,Q=4$ these are $g=2$ and $c=3$. We shall show that one cycle has $c$ samples, which visit $0,g,2g,\dots,n-g$ once each in some order; knowing which remainders occur will let us compare the sampled mean with the mean over all remainders. The argument has four steps. *Possible remainders.* Each remainder is $mQ$ minus a multiple of $n$, and both are divisible by $g$, so each remainder is a multiple of $g$. Between $0$ and $n-1$ there are $c$ such multiples, $0,g,2g,\dots,n-g$. *A return after $c$ steps.* Since $$ cQ=\frac ng Q=n\frac Qg, $$ taking another $c$ steps adds a multiple of $n$ and leaves the remainder unchanged. So $c$ is a period, and it remains to exclude an earlier repetition. *No earlier repetition.* Two integers have the same remainder on division by $n$ if and only if their difference is a multiple of $n$. For samples $m_1 ##### Compare means without calculating a new formula. Sorting the sampled remainders $4,2,0$ as $0,2,4$ leaves the sampled mean unchanged, and these remainders begin the pairs $(0,1)$, $(2,3)$, $(4,5)$. Since $(2^r-1)/(2^n-1)$ increases with $r$, the first remainder of each pair gives its smaller fractional part. We copy each sampled value twice and compare the copies with all six values of the consecutive cycle (Figure [1](#fig:cycle-mean)). ```{=latex} \begin{figure}[htbp] \centering % SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 % The arrow repeats values; it does not represent chronological sampling. % Each tuple is remainder/original numerator/repeated numerator, over 63. % Common linear height scale and equal widths preserve the comparison. \begin{tikzpicture}[x=1mm,y=1mm,font=\small] \node[anchor=west,align=left,inner sep=0pt] at (0,23) {3 sampled values\\(sorted)}; \node[anchor=west,inner sep=0pt] (samples) at (0,15) {$0,\ \dfrac{3}{63},\ \dfrac{15}{63}$}; % The arrow ends at the copied-value row, not at the original bar labels. \draw[-{Stealth[length=2mm]},line width=.6pt] ([yshift=-2mm]samples.south) -- (samples.south |- 0,-10.5) -- (61,-10.5); \node[anchor=west,inner sep=0pt] at (19,4) {copy each twice}; % Adjacent keys distinguish the constructed copies from the comparison data. \filldraw[fill=paperresultrule!30,draw=black!75,line width=.55pt] (33,20.75) rectangle (36.5,24.25); \node[anchor=west,align=left,inner sep=0pt] at (39,22.5) {copied sample\\values}; \draw[black!75,line width=.55pt] (33,12.75) rectangle (36.5,16.25); \node[anchor=west,align=left,inner sep=0pt] at (39,14.5) {consecutive\\cycle values}; \foreach \r/\v/\w in {0/0/0,1/1/0,2/3/3,3/7/3,4/15/15,5/31/15}{ \pgfmathsetmacro{\xx}{62+10*\r+3*floor(\r/2)} \fill[paperresultrule!30] (\xx,0) rectangle (\xx+7,.55*\w); \draw[black!75,line width=.55pt] (\xx,0) rectangle (\xx+7,.55*\v); \node[anchor=south,inner sep=1pt] at (\xx+3.5,.55*\v+1.3) {$\dfrac{\v}{63}$}; \node[anchor=north,inner sep=1pt] at (\xx+3.5,-1.3) {$\r$}; } \node[anchor=east,inner sep=0pt] at (58,-3) {remainder $r$}; \foreach \a in {62,85,108} \draw[decorate,decoration={brace,mirror,amplitude=3pt},black!65] (\a,-6.5) -- (\a+17,-6.5); % List the zero copies explicitly rather than inventing positive bar heights. \node[anchor=north,inner sep=1pt] at (70.5,-8.5) {$0,\ 0$}; \node[anchor=north,inner sep=1pt] at (93.5,-8.5) {$3/63,\ 3/63$}; \node[anchor=north,inner sep=1pt] at (116.5,-8.5) {$15/63,\ 15/63$}; \end{tikzpicture} \caption{For $n=6,Q=4$, two copies of each sample double both sum and count, preserving the mean. Each filled value is at most its outlined counterpart, so the sampled mean is at most the consecutive-cycle mean, which is below $1/6$.} \label{fig:cycle-mean} \end{figure} ``` [Figure 1 on page 9 of the PDF](https://wcook04.github.io/practical-formal-verification/papers/erdos257-expository-sums-never-fractions.pdf#page=9) · [SVG rendering](https://github.com/wcook04/lean-exposition/blob/main/papers/erdos257/expository/figures/cycle-mean.svg) In general each group consists of $g$ consecutive remainders, and the sample selects the first of them, giving $0,g,\dots,n-g$. Repeating each selected value $g$ times gives a sum no larger than the sum over all $n$ remainders. After division by $n$, the copied list has the mean of the $c$ samples, while the mean over the consecutive cycle is below $1/n$. Thus, whenever $M$ is a positive multiple of $c$, $$ \frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}\ell_n(mQ)<\frac1n. \tag{5} $$ The bound $1/n$ is independent of $Q$, so making the initial rows zero may require a large spacing without worsening it, provided $M$ completes the cycles. If $n$ divides $Q$, the cycle has the single entry $0$, which also satisfies the bound. ### 6.3 A bound that also covers unfinished cycles An unfinished cycle can miss its final zero. For $n=5$ and consecutive candidates ($Q=1$), one cycle is $$ \frac1{31},\quad\frac3{31},\quad\frac7{31},\quad\frac{15}{31},\quad0. $$ The first four entries average $26/(4\cdot31)=13/62>1/5$, whereas all five average $26/(5\cdot31)=26/155<1/5$, so the increasing positive list and the full cycle obey different bounds (Question [4](#chk:partial) gives a spaced example). Moreover, finitely many columns cannot complete infinitely many rows: if $n>MQ$, the last sample has not even reached the first positive multiple of $n$. We therefore need a second estimate, valid for *every* positive $M$: $$ \frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}\ell_n(mQ)\le\frac{2Q}{n}. \tag{6} $$ For fixed $Q$ this bound holds for every $M$, so choosing the number of columns later cannot invalidate it. We prove it with the same cycles. ##### First bound all the consecutive entries. The $M$ sampled exponents $Q,2Q,\dots,MQ$ lie among the first $MQ$ positive integers, and we first bound the sum over all $MQ$ entries. For $n\ge2$, consecutive entries beginning at $k=1$ repeat the block $$ \underbrace{\frac1{2^n-1},\frac3{2^n-1},\dots, \frac{2^{n-1}-1}{2^n-1}}_{n-1\text{ positive entries, increasing}},\quad 0. $$ For $n=2$ the positive list consists of $1/3$ alone. As the calculation for a complete cycle showed, the positive entries sum to less than $1$, so their average is less than $1/(n-1)$. No beginning portion of this *positive* list has a larger average, because each omitted entry is at least as large as every included entry, and appending the omitted entries therefore cannot lower the average. Thus a nonempty beginning portion has average at most $2/n$, since $1/(n-1)\le2/n$ for $n\ge2$. We left out the final zero for this comparison; the whole block, zero included, already has the stronger bound $1/n$. The first $MQ$ entries consist of complete blocks followed, possibly, by a beginning portion of the positive list; for $n=5$, for example, the first seven entries have numerators $(1,3,7,15,0)$ followed by $(1,3)$, all over $31$. Each piece has sum at most $2/n$ times its number of entries, and the pieces contain $MQ$ entries altogether, so their total is at most $2MQ/n$. For $n=1$ all entries are zero and the bound still holds. ##### Keep only the sampled entries. Removing nonnegative entries cannot increase the sum, and hence $$ \sum_{m=1}^{M}\ell_n(mQ) \le\sum_{k=1}^{MQ}\ell_n(k)\le\frac{2MQ}{n}. $$ Dividing by the number $M$ of candidates, we obtain [(6)](#eq:uniform-main). This also explains the factor $Q$: we bounded $M$ sampled entries by all $MQ$ consecutive entries. The candidates themselves are unchanged, and at no point did we assume that their sampled values increase.

rows.label: sec-intro
rows.text:
Every finite sum of fractions is a fraction, and an infinite sum can be one too:
$$
\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\dots=1.
$$
Now consider
$$
S=\frac13+\frac1{15}+\frac1{255}+\frac1{65535}+\dots,
$$
where the denominators are $2^2-1,2^4-1,2^8-1,2^{16}-1,\dots$ and the exponents double at each step. We will prove that this sum is equal to no fraction at all.

To see where such a proof might come from, multiply by $255$, the third denominator:
$$
\begin{aligned}
 255S&=85+17+1+\frac{255}{65535}+\dots\\
     &=103+\frac1{257}+\dots.
\end{aligned}
$$
The first three terms have become the integer $103$, and a positive remainder is left over. If $S=p/q$ with integers $p,q$ and $q>0$, then multiplying by an integer and subtracting an integer leaves an integer multiple of $1/q$, so a positive remainder must be at least $1/q$. Our plan is to repeat this construction until the *whole* remainder is smaller than that fixed gap, whatever denominator $q$ is proposed.

The example belongs to a larger family, whose fractions are obtained by taking a power of $2$, subtracting $1$, and taking the reciprocal:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|:--:|
| exponent $n$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $\dots$ |
| $2^n$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $16$ | $32$ | $64$ | $\dots$ |
| denominator $2^n-1$ | $1$ | $3$ | $7$ | $15$ | $31$ | $63$ | $\dots$ |
| term $1/(2^n-1)$ | $1$ | $\tfrac13$ | $\tfrac17$ | $\tfrac1{15}$ | $\tfrac1{31}$ | $\tfrac1{63}$ | $\dots$ |

Choose infinitely many of these terms, each at most once, and add them. Choosing the terms amounts to choosing a set $A$ of positive integer exponents. The opening example uses $A=\{2,4,8,16,\dots\}$, and choosing all even exponents instead gives
$$
A=\{2,4,6,8,\dots\}:\qquad
 \frac13+\frac1{15}+\frac1{63}+\frac1{255}+\dots.
$$
The exponent $0$ is excluded, since $2^0-1=0$, and we write
$$
S_A=\sum_{n\in A}\frac1{2^n-1}
$$
for the sum of the terms whose exponents belong to $A$, taken in increasing order of the exponents. A *partial sum* stops after finitely many selected terms, and to say that $S_A$ is *irrational* is to say that $S_A\ne p/q$ for all integers $p,q$ with $q>0$.

For the geometric series at the start, the partial sums are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|:---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| number of terms $N$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| $\tfrac12+\dots+\tfrac1{2^N}$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac34$ | $\tfrac78$ | $\tfrac{15}{16}$ |
| gap to $1$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac14$ | $\tfrac18$ | $\tfrac1{16}$ |

In general the partial sum is $1-2^{-N}$, and its gap to $1$ tends to zero; this is what the equation $\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18+\dots=1$ means.

Every series $S_A$ converges: for $n\ge1$,
$$
0<\frac1{2^n-1}\le\frac1{2^{n-1}},\qquad
 \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{n-1}}=2.
$$
The inequality follows from $2^n-1\ge2^{n-1}$, so the partial sums of $S_A$ increase and are bounded by $2$. A basic property of the real numbers says that an increasing bounded sequence has a finite limit (Appendix [A.1](#app:sums)), and the question is whether this limit is rational.

rows.label: sec-limits
rows.text:
For every integer $b\ge2$, the same method proves
$$
A\text{ infinite},\quad\sum_{n\in A}\frac1n<\infty
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sum_{n\in A}\frac1{b^n-1}\text{ is irrational}.
$$
We replace the multiplier by $b^k-1$; the fractional parts become $(b^{k\bmod n}-1)/(b^n-1)$, their cycle averages are still below $1/n$, and Appendix [A.5](#app:bases) checks both estimates.

The theorem covers every selection from the square-exponent series $1+\tfrac1{15}+\tfrac1{511}+\dots$. If infinitely many terms remain, their sum is irrational, because deleting terms cannot increase the reciprocal sum $\sum_{m\ge1}1/m^2<\infty$ of the exponents, so Theorem [1](#thm:main) still applies; if only finitely many remain, their sum is rational. Thus a selection from this series has a rational sum if and only if it is finite, whatever pattern the retained exponents follow, and the same holds with $2$ replaced by any integer $b\ge2$.

The reciprocal-sum condition is sufficient for irrationality, and the method stops short of necessity: the remainders $R(k)$ need not become arbitrarily small for every infinite $A$. When every positive exponent is selected, the terms with $n>k$ alone give
$$
R(k)\ge\sum_{n>k}\frac{2^k-1}{2^n-1}
 >\sum_{n>k}\frac{2^k-1}{2^n}
 =1-2^{-k}\ge\frac12.
$$
These remainders therefore never fall below $1/2$. Nevertheless, Erdős proved in 1948 that the full sum is irrational \[[1](#ref-erdos1948)\], and the failure of our method says nothing about rationality. Tao and Teräväinen proved irrationality for the prime exponents \[[5](#ref-taoteravainen2025), Theorem 1.3\], another case with divergent reciprocal sum. The short paper \[[6](#ref-shortpaper)\] gives further sufficient conditions, and the long record \[[7](#ref-longrecord)\] develops their proofs and the obstructions to extending them. Erdős’s question for every infinite set $A$ remains open.

Appendix [A.6](#app:lean) describes the formal proof of the theorem and how it differs from the finite-average proof given here.

rows.label: sec-problem
rows.text: In a 1988 account, Erdős wrote \[[3](#ref-erdos1988), p. 105\] (excerpt): > “let $n_1 **Theorem 1.** *Let $n_1

rows.label: sec-proof
rows.text: Suppose that $S=p/q$. Then every column total $R(k)$ is at least $1/q$, and we shall contradict this by making a finite average of column totals less than $1/q$. ### 7.1 The construction with actual numbers We use the doubling exponents once more, although we already have a shorter proof for them, because they let us watch the general method at work with actual numbers. Suppose the proposed denominator is $q=5$. It is enough to make the average of the column totals less than $1/5$, and we allow each of the two nonzero groups less than $1/10$. Beyond a doubling exponent $2^h$, the reciprocal tail is $1/2^{h+1}+1/2^{h+2}+\dots=1/2^h$. 1. *Decide which early rows to make zero.* Put the first cutoff at the exponent $t=16$. The reciprocal sum of all later rows is $1/16<1/10$, so any middle group fits within its allowance, whereas the earlier cutoff $8$ would give $1/8>1/10$. 2. *Preserve those zeros in every attempt.* Choose $Q=16$, which is divisible by $2,4,8,16$, so that every candidate $k=16m$ gives zero in these four rows. 3. *Make the infinite far group small despite the factor $2Q$.* Applying $2Q/n$ to every row beyond $t=16$ would bound the sum of their averages only by $32/16=2$, and raising a doubling cutoff $t$ together with $Q=t$ still gives $2Q/t=2$. This reflects a limitation of the estimate and says nothing about the size of $R(k)$. Instead we keep $Q=16$ and put the second cutoff at $T=512$, so that the remaining rows have exponents $1024,2048,\dots$, and adding the bounds $32/n$ on their averages gives $$ 32\left(\frac1{1024}+\frac1{2048}+\dots\right) =\frac{32}{512}<\frac1{10}. $$ A cutoff of $256$ would leave $32/256=1/8$, more than the allowance $1/10$. 4. *Complete all cycles between the cutoffs.* The middle exponents $32,64,128,256,512$ have cycle lengths $2,4,8,16,32$, and we choose $M=64$, a common multiple of these lengths. Every middle row then completes its cycles, and the far bound remains valid because it holds for every $M$. The cutoffs $t$ and $T$ are *values of exponents*, and they should be distinguished from counts of terms. The last candidate is $MQ=1024$ while the second cutoff is $T=512$, because the number of columns and the division of the rows into groups do different jobs. The choice $M=32$ would also work; taking $64$ shows that we may use more columns without changing either cutoff. The initial rows contribute zero, and the middle row averages together are less than $$ \frac1{32}+\frac1{64}+\frac1{128}+\frac1{256}+\frac1{512} =\frac{31}{512}. $$ The far row averages add up to at most $2Q/T=32/512$, and hence $$ \frac1{64}\sum_{m=1}^{64}R(16m) <\frac{31}{512}+\frac{32}{512}=\frac{63}{512}<\frac15. $$ At least one of the 64 complete attempts has $0 ### 7.2 The same choices for any admissible set Let $A$ satisfy the hypotheses of the theorem, and suppose that $S_A=p/q$, where $q$ is a positive integer. Only finitely many positive integers lie below any fixed bound, so the infinite set $A$ has arbitrarily large elements, and moving a cutoff farther out can only decrease a reciprocal tail. We may therefore take the cutoffs to be elements $tt}1/n<1/(2q)$, which is possible because the reciprocal tails tend to zero. 2. Choose a positive common multiple $Q$ of the selected exponents $n\le t$, for instance their product. These exponents divide every candidate $mQ$, so their rows are zero. 3. With $Q$ fixed, choose $T\in A$ with $T>t$ such that $2Q\sum_{n\in A,\,n>T}1/n<1/(2q)$; the tails tend to zero, and the coefficient $2Q$ is now fixed. 4. For the finitely many selected $tt}1/n<1/(2q)$ | | $n>T$ | bound $2Q/n$ for every $M$ | at most $2Q\sum_{n\in A,\,n>T}1/n<1/(2q)$ | By [(4)](#eq:average-main), the average of the column totals is therefore $$ \frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}R(mQ)<0+\frac1{2q}+\frac1{2q}=\frac1q. $$ At least one total is therefore below $1/q$, which contradicts the lower bound that rationality gives for every column. This proves Theorem [1](#thm:main). Looking back, infinitude supplied the positivity of the remainders, rationality supplied the fixed gap, and the convergence of $\sum_{n\in A}1/n$ supplied both small tails. The order of the choices ensured that all the bounds apply to the same finite collection of complete attempts.

rows.label: sec-split
rows.text: We want a multiplier that turns some terms into integers. Choose a positive integer $k$ and consider $2^k-1$; from now on $k$ is the exponent of the multiplier and no longer indexes the list $n_1,n_2,\dots$. For example, $15=2^4-1$ is divisible by $3=2^2-1$. Here is what multiplying by $15$ does to the first few terms: | | | | | | |:--------------:|:-------------:|:---------------:|:------------:|:---------------:| | exponent $n$ | original term | multiplied term | integer part | fractional part | | $2$ | $1/3$ | $15/3=5$ | $5$ | $0$ | | $3$ | $1/7$ | $15/7=2+1/7$ | $2$ | $1/7$ | | $4$ | $1/15$ | $15/15=1$ | $1$ | $0$ | | $5$ | $1/31$ | $15/31$ | $0$ | $15/31$ | The rows illustrate the operation, and in the chosen series we keep only the rows with $n\in A$. For $x\ge0$ the integer part $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the greatest integer at most $x$, and subtracting it leaves the fractional part $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1)$. For example, $2\le15/7<3$, so we subtract $2$ and keep $1/7$. Subtracting integer parts in this way keeps every contribution nonnegative. ##### The remainder can be read from the exponents. Keep the denominator $2^n-1$ fixed and add $n$ to $k$. Then the identity $$ 2^{k+n}-1=2^k(2^n-1)+(2^k-1) $$ gives $$ \frac{2^{k+n}-1}{2^n-1}=2^k+\frac{2^k-1}{2^n-1}. $$ The added term $2^k$ is an integer, so the fractional part is unchanged. Writing $k=an+r$ with $0\le r $$ \ell_n(k):=\left\{\frac{2^k-1}{2^n-1}\right\} =\frac{2^{k\bmod n}-1}{2^n-1}. \tag{2} $$ Here $k\bmod n$ denotes the remainder $r$ on division by $n$, which lies between $0$ and $n-1$, and $\ell_n(k)$ is the fractional part calculated from it; summing these fractional parts will give $R(k)$. For example, $8=2\cdot3+2$, so $\{255/7\}=(2^2-1)/7=3/7$. The fractional part vanishes when $n$ divides $k$ and only then, so the multiplier $2^k-1$ turns a selected term into an integer if and only if its exponent divides $k$. This is why we chose this multiplier: by taking $k$ divisible by some selected exponents, we make their contributions vanish. ##### What happens to the entire sum. We apply the same multiplier to every selected term, subtract each integer part, and sum the fractional parts: $$ R(k)=\sum_{n\in A}\ell_n(k),\qquad J(k)=\sum_{\substack{n\in A\\ n\le k}} \left\lfloor\frac{2^k-1}{2^n-1}\right\rfloor. $$ Only exponents $n\le k$ contribute to $J(k)$, since for $n>k$ the multiplied term is already less than $1$; thus $J(k)$ is a finite sum of integers. Splitting the terms gives $$ (2^k-1)S=J(k)+R(k). \tag{3} $$ The series defining $R(k)$ converges by comparison with $(2^k-1)S$, and Appendix [A.2](#app:split) justifies the identity using partial sums. The sum $R(k)$ may exceed $1$, so it need not be a fractional part itself. For the three exponents $2,3,6$ and $k=5$, the separate fractional parts sum to $$ \left\{\frac{31}3\right\}+\left\{\frac{31}7\right\} +\left\{\frac{31}{63}\right\} =\frac13+\frac37+\frac{31}{63}=\frac{79}{63}>1. $$ The fractional part of the whole product, by contrast, is $16/63$. We keep the separate contributions because each has the formula [(2)](#eq:fracpart-main), and their sum still has the required form $uS-j$. Finally, if $A$ is infinite, there is always a selected exponent $n>k$. Its multiplied term is positive and less than $1$, so it makes a positive contribution to $R(k)$, and all other contributions are nonnegative. Therefore $$ S=p/q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R(k)=(2^k-1)S-J(k)\ge\frac1q\quad\hbox{for every }k\ge1. $$ Our task is now to find *one* $k$ with $R(k)<1/q$ (Question [2](#chk:positive)).

rows.label: sec-test
rows.text: Start with $2/5$. Multiplying it by an integer and subtracting an integer always gives an integer multiple of $1/5$: $$ 3\cdot\frac25-1=\frac15,\quad 4\cdot\frac25-1=\frac35,\quad 5\cdot\frac25-2=0,\quad 1\cdot\frac25-1=-\frac35. $$ No such value lies strictly between $0$ and $1/5$, because the denominator fixes a smallest possible positive result. The same reasoning applies to any fraction. From now on we write $S=S_A$ for the series belonging to our chosen set $A$ and suppose that $S=p/q$, where $p\in\mathbb Z$ and $q$ is a positive integer. For integers $u,j$, $$ uS-j=\frac{up-jq}{q}. $$ The numerator is an integer, so if $uS-j>0$, then $up-jq\ge1$ and $$ uS-j\ge\frac1q. $$ Positivity matters here, since zero and negative values are perfectly compatible with rationality. To prove our sum irrational, we shall therefore suppose that $S=p/q$ and construct integers $u,j$, which may depend on $q$, such that $$ 0

rows.label: a-weighted-condition-on-the-support
rows.text: A prime-power factor can compensate for a large sum of reciprocals of cofactors. If $a=2^km$ with $m$ odd, the weighted term below is $1/[m(b^{2^k}-1)]$, so the support may contain increasingly many odd cofactors as $k$ grows while the weighted sum stays finite. The following theorem extends this observation to a finite set of primes. **Theorem 1.1 (A weighted summability criterion).** *Let $b\ge2$ be an integer, let $\mathcal P$ be a finite nonempty set of primes, and let $A\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}$ be infinite. Write* $$ h(a)=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{v_p(a)}, $$ *where $v_p(a)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $a$; thus $h(a)$ is the $\mathcal P$-part of $a$. If* $$ W_{b,\mathcal P}(A):= \sum_{a\in A}\frac{h(a)}{a\bigl(b^{h(a)}-1\bigr)}<\infty, \tag{1} $$ *then* $$ X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{b^a-1} $$ *is irrational. More precisely, for* $$ \Delta_{b,A}(m)= \sum_{a\in A}\frac{b^{m\bmod a}-1}{b^a-1}, $$ *for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $N$ there is an $m\ge N$ with $0<\Delta_{b,A}(m)<\varepsilon$.* ###### Examples and limits of the hypothesis. Squares, powers of two and factorials have summable reciprocals and therefore satisfy the base-two weighted condition. Full support fails it, since for any fixed finite prime set $P$ its subset coprime to $\prod_{p\in P}p$ has weight $1/[a(b-1)]$ and divergent reciprocal sum. The set of all odd exponents fails for the same reason, as we see by restricting to integers coprime to $2\prod_{p\in P}p$, and inclusion–exclusion in the harmonic sum proves both divergences. These failures limit the sufficient condition only, and full support is in any case known to be irrational. Writing $a=hm$ with $h$ its $\mathcal P$-part gives the exact decomposition $$ W_{b,\mathcal P}(A)=\sum_{h\in\mathcal H_{\mathcal P}}\frac1{b^h-1} \sum_{\substack{m\ge1,\ hm\in A\\(m,\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p)=1}}\frac1m, $$ where $\mathcal H_{\mathcal P}$ consists of $1$ and the positive integers with no prime factor outside $\mathcal P$. A finite weighted sum therefore forces each inner reciprocal sum to be finite, and the outer sum imposes a further summability condition across different $\mathcal P$-parts. For example, at base two with $\mathcal P=\{2\}$, we may choose in each layer $2^k$, $k\ge1$, a finite set of odd factors whose reciprocal sum is at least $2^{2^k}$, which is possible because the harmonic sum over odd integers diverges. Every inner sum is then finite while the outer weighted sum diverges. Prime support also fails the criterion for every finite $\mathcal P$, since the primes outside $\mathcal P$ contribute a constant multiple of their divergent reciprocal sum. As before, these failures concern the sufficient hypothesis and say nothing about rationality of the resulting values. Nevertheless the condition is strictly weaker than reciprocal summability, as the following construction shows. At base two take $$ A_\star=\{2^k m:k\ge1,\ m\text{ odd},\ m\le2^{2^k}\}. $$ Write $H_N=\sum_{m=1}^N1/m$ and $N_k=2^{2^k}$. The sum of reciprocals of the exponents with $v_2(a)=k$ is $$ \rho_k=2^{-k}\!\sum_{\substack{m\le N_k\\m\text{ odd}}}\frac1m =2^{-k}\bigl(H_{N_k}-\tfrac12H_{N_k/2}\bigr) \longrightarrow\frac{\log2}{2}. $$ Thus $\sum_{a\in A_\star}1/a$ diverges. For $\mathcal P=\{2\}$, the weighted contribution of the same layer is $$ \frac{2^k}{2^{2^k}-1}\rho_k. $$ Since $H_N\le1+\log N$, these terms are at most $(1+2^k\log2)2^{1-2^k}$, which is summable. The theorem therefore proves irrationality at every integer base for every infinite subset of this set, although its reciprocal sum diverges. *Proof.* We first derive the lower bound that rationality imposes and then estimate a finite average of the same quantities. Division of $m$ by $a$, say $m=qa+r$ with $0\le r $$ \Delta_{b,A}(m)=(b^m-1)X_A(b)-J_{b,A}(m), \qquad J_{b,A}(m)= \sum_{\substack{a\in A\\a\le m}} \sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor m/a\rfloor}b^{m-ja}\in\mathbb Z. \tag{2} $$ The integer sum is finite. Moreover $\Delta_{b,A}(m)>0$ for $m\ge1$, since $A$ is infinite and so some $a\in A$ exceeds $m$ and contributes a positive summand, while at $m=0$ the displacement is zero. Thus, if $X_A(b)=u/v$ with $v>0$, equation [(2)](#eq:257-weighted-lattice) gives $v\Delta_{b,A}(m)\in\mathbb Z$, whence $$ \Delta_{b,A}(m)\ge \frac1v\qquad(m\ge1). \tag{3} $$ We therefore seek positive indices at which the displacement is arbitrarily small. Put $$ \phi_a(m)=\frac{b^{m\bmod a}}{b^a-1}, \qquad d_a(m)=\phi_a(m)-\frac1{b^a-1}. $$ Then $d_a(m)\ge0$ and $\Delta_{b,A}(m)=\sum_{a\in A}d_a(m)$. For $Q,a,T\ge1$, put $g=(Q,a)$. The residues $tQ\bmod a$ have period $a/g$ and visit $0,g,\ldots,a-g$ once in a period, so $$ \sum_{t=1}^{a/g}\phi_a(tQ) =\frac{1+b^g+\cdots+b^{a-g}}{b^a-1} =\frac1{b^g-1}. $$ Splitting the average into complete periods and at most one incomplete period, we obtain $$ \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_a(tQ) \le \frac{g}{a(b^g-1)}+\frac1{T(b^g-1)}. \tag{4} $$ The complete-period term is the source of the weight in [(1)](#eq:257-weighted-mass), since replacing $g$ by the $\mathcal P$-part $h(a)$ gives its summand. The modulus chosen below permits this replacement when $h(a)\le H$, and larger prime parts receive a separate estimate. The comparison uses the fact that $n/(b^n-1)$ decreases for positive integers $n$; indeed $$ n(b^{n+1}-1)-(n+1)(b^n-1) =b^n\bigl(n(b-1)-1\bigr)+1>0. $$ Exponents beyond the observation range admit a uniform bound. If $Y=QT$ and $a>Y\ge tQ$, then $tQ\bmod a=tQ$ and $d_a(tQ)\le2\,2^{tQ-a}$. Hence $$ \sum_{a>Y}d_a(tQ)\le2\,2^{tQ-Y}, \qquad \sum_{t=1}^{T}2^{tQ-Y} =\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}2^{-jQ}\le2, $$ and therefore $$ \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{\substack{a\in A\\a>QT}}d_a(tQ)\le\frac4T. \tag{5} $$ The incomplete-period term in [(4)](#eq:257-weighted-gcd-average) carries no factor $1/a$, and although it tends to zero for each fixed exponent, the number of observed exponents grows with the window. We recover a summable bound by averaging over window lengths and summing in the other order. An exponent $a$ first enters when the window reaches $a/Q$, and with geometrically spaced lengths the reciprocals of all later lengths sum to at most $2Q/a$. Let $\alpha_a\ge0$ with $\sum_a\alpha_a/a<\infty$. For $Q,M\ge1$, finite rearrangement gives $$ \sum_{j=M}^{2M-1}\frac1{2^j} \sum_{a\le Q2^j}\alpha_a \le 2Q\sum_{a\ge1}\frac{\alpha_a}{a}. \tag{6} $$ Indeed, for each fixed $a$ the admissible indices satisfy $2^j\ge a/Q$ and $$ \sum_{\substack{M\le j<2M\\a\le Q2^j}}2^{-j}\le\frac{2Q}{a}. $$ Only finitely many terms occur on the left, so the rearrangement is a finite one. We now choose the modulus to be divisible by a fixed finite subset of the support and by all powers of primes in $\mathcal P$ up to a growing threshold. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and a lower bound $N$, and select a finite $F\subseteq A$ such that $$ \sum_{a\in A\mathbin{\backslash} F} \frac{h(a)}{a(b^{h(a)}-1)}<\varepsilon, \tag{7} $$ and put $L=\operatorname{lcm}(F)$, with $L=1$ if $F$ is empty. Write $p_*=\max\mathcal P$ and $r=|\mathcal P|$. For a large integer $H\ge2p_*$, set $$ Q_0(H)=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{\lfloor\log_pH\rfloor}, \qquad Q=LQ_0(H), \qquad G=\left\lfloor\frac H{p_*}\right\rfloor. $$ Then $Q\le LH^r$, $G\ge1$, and every $a\in F$ divides $Q$, so its $d_a(tQ)$ contribution vanishes. Consider first $a\in A\mathbin{\backslash} F$ with $a\le QT$ and $h(a)\le H$. Every prime-power factor of $h(a)$ occurs in $Q_0(H)$, hence $h(a)\mid Q_0(H)$ and $(Q,a)\ge h(a)$. By [(4)](#eq:257-weighted-gcd-average) and the monotonicity above, the total contribution of these $a$ is therefore at most $$ \varepsilon+ \frac1T\sum_{\substack{a\in A, a\le QT\\h(a)\le H}} \frac1{b^{h(a)}-1}. \tag{8} $$ The first term comes from the tail bound [(7)](#eq:257-weighted-tail-choice). For $h(a)>H$ we have $(Q,a)\ge G$. If every $\mathcal P$-prime-power component of $h(a)$ is at most $H$, then $h(a)\mid Q_0(H)$ and the gcd is larger than $H$. Otherwise some $p^{v_p(a)}>H$, and the gcd contains $p^{\lfloor\log_pH\rfloor}>H/p\ge H/p_*$. Once we enlarge the sum in [(4)](#eq:257-weighted-gcd-average) from the support to all $a\le QT$, it bounds the large-$h(a)$ part by $$ \frac{G(1+\log(QT))+Q}{b^G-1}; \tag{9} $$ we used $\sum_{a\le QT}a^{-1}\le1+\log(QT)$ and $\#\{a\le QT\}/T=Q$. Let $$ \mathcal M(Q,T)=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Delta_{b,A}(tQ). $$ Combining [(5)](#eq:257-weighted-outer), [(8)](#eq:257-weighted-small-part), and [(9)](#eq:257-weighted-large-part) gives $$ \mathcal M(Q,T)\le \varepsilon+ \frac1T\sum_{\substack{a\in A, a\le QT\\h(a)\le H}} \frac1{b^{h(a)}-1} +\frac{G(1+\log(QT))+Q}{b^G-1}+\frac4T. \tag{10} $$ Increasing the number $M$ of dyadic lengths reduces the incomplete-period error to order $Q/M$, but it also makes $\log T$ of order $M$ on the largest window and so raises the large-gcd contribution to order $GM/b^G$. Both quantities must therefore be made small together. With $L$ fixed, $Q$ grows polynomially in $H$ and $G$ grows linearly, so an intermediate exponential choice of $M$ achieves both. We choose $$ M=\left\lfloor b^{G/2}\right\rfloor $$ and average [(10)](#eq:257-weighted-master-average) over $T=2^j$, $M\le j<2M$, and apply [(6)](#eq:257-weighted-dyadic-average) with $\alpha_a={\bf1}_A(a)/(b^{h(a)}-1)$. Its hypothesis holds because $$ \sum_a\frac{\alpha_a}{a} =\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a(b^{h(a)}-1)} \le W_{b,\mathcal P}(A). $$ The resulting finite average satisfies $$ \frac1M\sum_{j=M}^{2M-1}\mathcal M(Q,2^j) \le \varepsilon+\frac{2QW_{b,\mathcal P}(A)}M +\frac{G(1+\log Q+2M\log2)+Q}{b^G-1} +4\,2^{-M}. \tag{11} $$ As $H\to\infty$, $$ Q\le LH^r,\qquad G=H/p_*+O(1),\qquad M\asymp b^{G/2}. $$ Consequently $Q/M\to0$, $GM/b^G\to0$, $(G\log Q+Q)/b^G\to0$, and $2^{-M}\to0$. For sufficiently large $H$, we may also arrange $Q\ge N$ and make the right side of [(11)](#eq:257-weighted-final-diagonal) smaller than $2\varepsilon$. The left side is a finite average of the positive numbers $\Delta_{b,A}(tQ)$, so one of them satisfies $$ 0<\Delta_{b,A}(tQ)<2\varepsilon, \qquad tQ\ge Q\ge N. $$ Since $\varepsilon$ was an arbitrary positive number, applying the construction with $\varepsilon/2$ gives the stated cofinal bound with $\Delta_{b,A}(m)<\varepsilon$. This contradicts [(3)](#eq:257-weighted-gap) if $X_A(b)$ is rational. ◻ Since $b^{h(a)}-1\ge2^{h(a)}-1$ for every $b\ge2$, one has $W_{b,\mathcal P}(A)\le W_{2,\mathcal P}(A)$. Hence the base-two weighted hypothesis gives the conclusion at every integer base simultaneously, and it passes to infinite subsets. The theorem reaches only supports in the weighted class and gives no quantitative irrationality measure, and we claim no priority for it. ###### Averaging antecedents. Both averaging proofs in this section end by choosing a term no larger than a finite mean. [Duverney and Tachiya](https://danielduverney.fr/documents/theorie-des-nombres/DuverneyTachiya190522.pdf) choose their index in the same way in their refinement of the Chowla–Erdős method, where they average a local coefficient mass over an arithmetic progression built by the Chinese remainder theorem and a term attaining the minimum supplies the bounds that control the tail beyond it (Section 2, (2.3)–(2.9), pp. 5–6 of the author preprint). [Kaneko, Suzuki and Tachiya](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20743) measure the average decay of scaled tails by $R_c(q,x,z)$, their (1.7) on p. 3 of arXiv v1. Under a counting condition on the support and a bound on $R_c$, most scaled tails in a range are small, and arbitrarily small nonzero scaled tails give irrationality (Lemmas 1 and 2, pp. 6–8). Their sparsity refers to the positions of nonzero power-series coefficients, and for our series these stay dense however sparse the selected Lambert denominators are, since the divisor-incidence coefficients $\#\{a\in A:a\mid n\}$ are positive on every multiple of $\min A$. For any splitting into two sequences, the two coefficient supports therefore cover a set of positive lower density, which is incompatible with the support-counting conditions \[[6](#ref-kanekosuzukitachiya), Theorem 1(iii), p. 3, and Theorem 3(iv), p. 5\] requiring both counts to be $o(x_n/z_n)$ with $z_n\ge1$. Their remote-tail quantity $R_c(q,x,z)$ sums only offsets $j\ge z$, whereas the full scaled tail $$ \sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\#\{a\in A:a\mid m+r\}}{b^r} =\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(m)=X_A(b)+\Delta_{b,A}(m) $$ is at least $X_A(b)$, which gives no lower bound for $R_c$. The proofs above therefore average the displacement itself, along multiples of a modulus that freezes a finite part of $A$, and the weighted proof adds the dyadic average [(6)](#eq:257-weighted-dyadic-average).

rows.label: abstract
rows.text: **Abstract.** We prove that $\sum_{a\in A}(b^a-1)^{-1}$ is irrational for every integer $b\ge2$ and every infinite $A\subseteq E\cup V$, whenever the set $E$ satisfies a finite-prime weighted summability condition at base two and $V$ admits a summable positive divisor cover. Since the estimates for the two sets hold on one finite distribution, the union criterion reaches supports that lie in neither individual class. We also develop the arithmetic of finite denominators, the geometry of the achievement set and integer-quotient tests for $1/2$ and $1/21$, keeping each conditional argument with its hypotheses, each computation with its finite range and each counterexample with the estimate it refutes. Whether $1/2$ and $1/21$ are subseries sums, and the unrestricted base-two problem, remain open.

rows.label: combining-the-two-support-criteria
rows.text: A sequence of indices with small weighted displacements and another with small covered displacements could be disjoint, so their small values need never occur at the same index. We therefore let the weighted proof choose one finite distribution, and the explicit modulus dependence in [(13)](#eq:257-mixed-finite-kernel) allows the cover estimate to use the same distribution. We add the two nonnegative errors on that distribution and choose an index only afterwards. **Theorem 1.4 (mixed weighted and cover supports).** *Let $E,V\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{>0}$. Suppose $E$ has finite weighted mass [(1)](#eq:257-weighted-mass) at $b=2$ for a finite nonempty prime set $\mathcal P$. Suppose also that $V\subseteq\bigcup_jF_j$ for sets and majorants satisfying Theorem [1.3](#thm:257-variable-fractional-cover), with [(14)](#eq:257-strengthened-cover) or its positive-weight variant. Then $X_A(b)$ is irrational for every infinite $A\subseteq E\cup V$ and every integer $b\ge2$.* *Proof.* Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and an integer $N_0\ge1$, and put $\rho=\varepsilon/3$. We use the cover notation $B_j,U_j,V_j$ above, with $\eta_j=2^{-j}$ in the case [(14)](#eq:257-strengthened-cover). Set $t_j=\rho\eta_j$ and choose $J$ so that $$ K_J=\sum_{j>J}\frac{C_jt_j^{-\alpha_j}}{B_j-1}<\frac1{16}. $$ Choose a finite $F\subseteq E$ whose complementary weighted mass is $\kappa<\rho/16$. Let $L$ be a positive common multiple of $N_0$, all members of $F$, and all members of the first $J$ covering sets. The order of choices matters. The finite pieces determine $L$, the weighted argument then enlarges $L$ to $Q$ and chooses the dyadic scales, and a sample is selected only after both estimates hold on that distribution. With the finite sets and $L$ fixed, we choose the base-two weighted parameters $$ Q=L\prod_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{\lfloor\log_pH\rfloor},\qquad G=\lfloor H/\max\mathcal P\rfloor,\qquad M=\lfloor2^{G/2}\rfloor. $$ All the following estimates use $\mathscr D_{Q;M,M}$, whose scales run from $M$ to $2M-1$, and both quantities are evaluated at the same sampled multiple $N=Qm$. The finite estimate [(11)](#eq:257-weighted-final-diagonal), with complementary weighted mass $\kappa$, remains valid for this $L$, because its proof requires only that every member of $F$ divide $L$. It also applies when $E$ is finite or empty, since positivity was used only after the averaging estimate. Thus $$ \mathscr D_{Q;M,M}(\Delta_{2,E}/\rho)<\frac18 $$ for sufficiently large $H$. For the same finite distribution, [(13)](#eq:257-mixed-finite-kernel) and nonnegative interchange give $$ \mathscr D_{Q;M,M}S_J\le(1+4Q/M)K_J<\frac18, \qquad S_J=\sum_{j>J}t_j^{-\alpha_j}V_j, $$ because $Q/M\to0$. Here the cover estimate is applied with the enlarged modulus $Q$ in place of the fixed divisor $L$, which is why its explicit modulus dependence was needed. On this single distribution, therefore, $$ \mathscr D_{Q;M,M}(\Delta_{2,E}/\rho+S_J)<\frac14. $$ We choose a sampled $N=Qm$ at which the nonnegative sum is less than $1$. Since both quantities and every summand of $S_J$ are nonnegative, this gives $\Delta_{2,E}(N)<\rho$ and $U_j(N)J$. For $j\le J$, it is the displacement $\Delta_{2,F_j}(N)$ that vanishes, since every exponent in $F_j$ divides $L$ and hence divides $N$. Therefore $$ \Delta_{2,A}(N)\le\Delta_{2,E}(N)+\Delta_{2,V}(N)<2\rho<\varepsilon, \qquad N\ge Q\ge L\ge N_0. $$ The inequality also holds when $E$ and $V$ overlap. Since $A$ is infinite, $\Delta_{b,A}(N)>0$, and the comparison $\Delta_{b,A}(N)\le\Delta_{2,A}(N)$ from the cover proof makes these values arbitrarily small at every integer base, which contradicts the positive lower bound imposed by rationality. ◻ ###### Why the mixed criterion is strict. Take an infinite support $E$ satisfying the weighted condition but admitting no strengthened positive cover, and an infinite support $V$ admitting such a cover but failing the weighted condition for every finite prime set at every integer base. Such sets are supplied by the two constructions in the short paper’s section comparing support classes. Put $U=E\cup V$. A strengthened cover of $U$ would restrict to one of $E$, since each divisor count decreases on passing to a subset, and convergence of the weighted sum over $U$ would imply convergence over $V$ with the same prime set, since every summand is nonnegative. Hence $U$ belongs to neither individual class. For every infinite $A\subseteq U$, however, Theorem [1.4](#thm:257-mixed-supports) applies with the same sets $E,V$ and gives irrationality at every integer base, a conclusion that irrationality of the two summands separately would not supply. This proves the short paper’s strictness corollary from the two constructions, subject to the ordinary-proof qualification stated below. The positive-weight variant of Theorem [1.3](#thm:257-variable-fractional-cover), with its hereditary all-base conclusion, also has a [kernel-checked Lean proof](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/c91562bd574a387cde904481e609c7b4cacebb14/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/PaperCompleteR8/ArbitraryWeightMixedClaim.lean#L19). To exhibit a support outside both individual classes, the preceding strictness argument needs the two separating constructions in addition to Theorem [1.4](#thm:257-mixed-supports). The existence of two sets with the required properties has a [Lean proof](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/3973d3b10bce72017b8f60093f0d6c3f4f592d80/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/PaperCompleteR8/AnalyticIncomparability.lean#L53) in which the second set is formed from squarefree divisor sets with a different choice of parameters. The printed fresh-prime construction and the strictness corollary have ordinary proofs, and none of these constructions has been independently reviewed. The second set in the Lean proof also admits no cover with $\sum_jC_j2^{j\alpha_j}2^{\alpha_j}/(2^{\alpha_j}-1)^2<\infty$, so this stronger cost defines a [strictly smaller support class](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/3973d3b10bce72017b8f60093f0d6c3f4f592d80/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/PaperCompleteR8/AnalyticIncomparability.lean#L41). The mixed implication itself is kernel-checked. Universal irrationality and the quantitative and prime-power thinning claims remain open. Supports satisfying the mixed criterion are closed under finite unions and finite changes, even with the fixed dyadic cover cost in [(14)](#eq:257-strengthened-cover). For two covers, we interleave their $j$th finite sets at positions $2j-1,2j$ and halve each exponent, which compensates for the increased index in $2^{j\alpha_j}$. The same coefficients still majorise the smaller powers, since integer divisor counts satisfy $f^{\alpha/2}\le f^\alpha$. The only remaining cost is the denominator $2^\alpha-1$, and replacing $\alpha$ by $\alpha/2$ increases the full cost of each finite set by at most $1+\sqrt2$. For $r$ covers, positions at most $rj$ and exponents divided by $r$ give a cost ratio below $2r$. For weighted supports we take the union of the finite prime sets, under which the prime part can only increase while $h/(2^h-1)$ decreases. Each condition passes to subsets, and the weighted sum is finite on a finite support. [Lean proves](https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos/blob/3973d3b10bce72017b8f60093f0d6c3f4f592d80/lean/ErdosProblems/Erdos257/PaperCompleteR8/StrengthenedCoverFiniteUnion.lean#L167) these closures with the constant $3$ in place of $1+\sqrt2$. For a countable union the cover costs must still be summable. Every prime singleton is admitted, but for the full prime support $\mathcal P$ we have $\Delta_{2,\mathcal P}(N)>1/3$ for every $N\ge1$, because $\sum_{r\ge1}2^{-r}\omega(N+r)\ge1$ while $X_{\mathcal P}(2)\le\sum_{a\ge2}(2^a-1)^{-1}<2/3$, where $\omega(n)$ is the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$. ###### The elementary independence boundary. For the divisor counts $c_A$ and a fixed $a\in A$, the identity $c_A(an)-c_A(n)=1-\mathbf1_{a\mid n}$ holds for every $n\ge1$ exactly when $a$ is coprime to every other member of $A$. Indeed, every summand $\mathbf1_{t\mid an}-\mathbf1_{t\mid n}$ is nonnegative, the term $t=a$ supplies the right side, and coprimality makes all other terms zero, while if $g=(a,t)>1$ for some $t\ne a$, the choice $n=t/g$ produces an additional positive term. For distinct odd primes $p,q$, the covariance of $\mathbf1_{2p\mid n}$ and $\mathbf1_{2q\mid n}$ over a common period is $1/(2pq)-1/(4pq)=1/(4pq)$. Thus dilating a prime support already destroys the independence used in the prime-incidence argument. This short ordinary calculation bounds the reach of that argument and has no irrationality consequence of its own.

rows.label: conditional-membership-tests
rows.text: The finite tests below use $g_n=w_n-R_n$. When written as functions, $R(n)=R_n$, $g(n)=g_n$, $r(x,n)=r_n(x)$ and $C(A,N)=C_A(N)$. For a finite set $D$, $V(D)=X_D(2)$. For $n\ge2$, the integer remainder $s(n)=\mathrm{rem}(n)$ uses weights $q(2n,d)$, $2\le d **Theorem 6.1 (Infinitely many greedy skips force membership).** *Fix $x\ge0$. If $r_n(x)>R_n$ at some rank $n$, every later rank is selected and $r_{n+k}(x)>R_{n+k}$ for every $k\ge0$.
